subject: Multiple random effect and regularization in LMM

messages.author: 21b39e2b255e81ed
messages.subject: Multiple random effect and regularization in LMM
parts:
I am new to STAN but so far have enjoyed using it so much,
I didn't find examples regarding LMM with multiple random effect in the STAN's manual however, found Bayesian linear mixed model using STAN helpful; even though their example is neither multivariate nor have multiple random effect. 

The experiment is as following,
We have monitored 3 groups of mice each consisting of 12 animal for 10 weeks. During each week, we have measured the abundance of 250 bacteria in each mouse along with the animal's body weight. 

One of the questions I would like to answer is, which bacteria can predict the body weight regardless of the condition. Therefore, I built an LMM, where bacteria are fixed effects whereas, the week_number and the condition are random effects. I assume each animal has it's own intercept and slope;

My question here, are 1) have I formulated my question right within stan , 2) how effectively I can impose shrinkage (e.g LASSO) on the LMM. 


data {
     int<lower=0> Nobs; // number of subjects
     int<lower=0> Ntaxa; // number of taxa
     int<lower=0> Nanimals; //number of animals
     int<lower=0> Ncondition; //number of condition
     vector[Nobs] y; //body weight
     matrix[Nobs,Ntaxa] x; // abundance matrix
     int<lower=1,upper=Nanimals> animal[Nobs];
     int<lower=1,upper=Nanimals> condition[Nobs];
}

parameters {
  vector[Ntaxa] beta;
  real<lower=0> sigmaint;
  real<lower=0> sigmaslope;
  real<lower=0> sigmaeps;

  vector[Nanimals] etaint_animal;
  vector[Nanimals] etaslope_animal;
  
  vector[Ncondition] etaint_condition;
  vector[Ncondition] etaslope_condition;
}

transformed parameters {
  vector[Nanimals] ranint_animal;
  vector[Nanimals] ranslope_animal;
  vector[Nobs] raneff_animal;

  vector[Ncondition] ranint_condition;
  vector[Ncondition] ranslope_condition;
  vector[Nobs] raneff_condition;

  ranint_animal = sigmaint * etaint_animal; //size : number of anuimals
  ranslope_animal = sigmaslope * etaslope_animal;//size : numer of animals
  
  ranslope_condition = sigmaslope * etaslope_condition;//size : numer of condition
  ranint_condition = sigmaslope * etaslope_condition;//size : numer of condition
  
  for (i in 1:Nobs)
  {
    raneff_animal[i] = ranint_animal[animal[i]]+ranslope_animal[animal[i]];
    raneff_condition[i] = ranint_condition[condition[i]]+ranslope_condition[condition[i]];
  }

}
model {
  y ~ lognormal(x * beta + raneff_animal + raneff_condition, sigmaeps);
  etaint_animal ~ normal(0, 3);
  etaslope_animal ~ normal(0, 3);
}

generated quantities {
  vector[Nobs] log_lik;
  for (n in 1:Nobs)
  {
    log_lik[n] = lognormal_log(y[n], x[n] * beta, sigmaeps);
  }
}

Regarding the shrinkage, if I understood correctly in the manual (page 546), one just need to multiple a "negative lambda" by "the absolute of coefficients"; Is there any non-parametric way to estimate shrinkage parameter "\lambda" as well, given my linear mixed model.

Thanks

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Multiple random effect and regularization in LMM
parts:
If you're fitting penalized maximum likelihood with the lasso,
you'll have problem with mixed models because they typically don't
have maximum likelihood estimates --- you need to move to max
marginal likelihood like in the lme4 package on R (Andrew and
Dustin are working on adding max marginal likelihood estimation to
Stan, but it's still at the prototype stage).

Usually you don't want slope parameters in linear models to
be constrained positive as you've done with sigmaslope.

Also, when you have expressions like this:
> y ~ lognormal(x * beta + raneff_animal + raneff_condition, sigmaeps);

you will immediately have an identifiability problem as discussed
in the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual.

If you have random slopes and intercepts, you can provide a joint
multivaraite prior for them. But the slope, to be a slope, should
be multiplied by a covariate. What you've done is produced a model
with two intercepts, one named ranint and one named ranslope.

- Bob
